items.title: Ukraine’s drone strikes spur hasty Russian plans for underground data centers
items.author: Jeremy Hsu
items.content: Russian tech companies are scrambling to harden and hide their data centers underground after Ukrainian drone strikes damaged facilities housing AI supercomputers and disrupted cloud services for millions of Russian users. Meanwhile, the Kremlin is requiring data center owners to reserve computing capacity for emergency state needs and has even authorized possible use of foreign data centers. These consequences of Russia's war against Ukraine come as the Russian military has bombarded Ukrainian cities with drones and missiles nearly night and day in recent months, along with specifically targeting Ukrainian data centers since late September. But Ukraine has retaliated with its own drone strikes on military and infrastructure targets across Russia, degrading or knocking out data centers operated by Russian tech giant Yandex, the state-owned bank Sberbank, social media site VKontakte, and the Russian Ministry of Finance. Now, state-owned telecommunications company Rostelcom has raised the possibility of moving some Russian data centers underground in talks with the nickel and palladium mining company Norilsk, according to Russian newspaper Vedomosti. The industry publication Data Center Dynamics also pointed to a recent proposal by a Russian regional governor to build data centers within open-pit coal mines while planting green public parks above as camouflage. items.title: Postal Service Surveilled Protest Activities Online With Little Rules, Oversight
items.author: Aaron Mackey
items.content: The U.S. Postal Service used social media surveillance to monitor and report on protests across the political spectrum, government records show. The records, disclosed to EFF and other requesters suing the postal service under the Freedom of Information Act, show that the agency’s internet Covert Operations Program, or iCOP, routinely sifted through social media posts organizing and discussing protests with little records of any oversight or legal justification. EFF filed suit in 2021 after Yahoo News disclosed the program’s existence and how the agency used it to monitor First Amendment protected activities. After years of delays and technical failures that led the agency to lose access to a trove of emails discussing the program, the postal service disclosed records to EFF and several other requesters this year. The Postal Service used iCOP to surveil First Amendment activities The disclosures include a series of bulletins created from iCOP, which show that the postal service used the program in 2020 and 2021 to monitor and circulate information about a wide range of planned protests. They included a planned “Million MAGA March,” a guns rights advocacy event and counter-protest in Virginia, a nationwide Save the Post Office Saturday protest, and planned protests in front of then-Postmaster General Louis DeJoy’s home in Washington, D.C. Many of the bulletins provide dry descriptions of the events being planned and reference public discussions or events on major social media services. Others seem to imply or anticipate that the protests would turn violent. For example, in discussing planned national and international protests scheduled for March 20, 2021, the bulletin references potential violence in light of “online inflammatory material.” Yet the bulletin acknowledges that the agency has “no intelligence to suggest specific threats.” This bulletin was described by Yahoo News when it disclosed iCOP’s existence. Another bulletin discussing an ongoing Black Lives Matter protests in response to police shooting and killing people styles itself as a “National Civil Unrest Update.” The bulletins also recount and monitor threats sent to then-Postmaster DeJoy. The Postal Service also disclosed three email chains to EFF that, while heavily redacted, show how the agency queried iCOP and disseminated what it found (Read the emails here, here, and here). The government agreed to release the email messages as part of settling EFF’s FOIA suit this fall. To EFF’s knowledge, they are the only existing materials that reflect how the agency queried iCOP. Postal Service renames iCOP and loses access to records about it According to the agency, after Yahoo News disclosed the program in 2021, the postal service renamed it and publicly said that it had stopped issuing bulletins. But the documents do not say that the agency’s social media surveillance stopped. At the same time, EFF and several other FOIA requesters sought records detailing how the agency used iCOP and what rules the postal service had for using the program and distributing information it gained from surveilling social media. EFF spent years pushing the agency to disclose email communications about the program, which the agency had stored on an external hard drive. Amid these negotiations, someone dropped the hard drive, rendering it inoperable, agency officials said. By the time that happened, the agency had already deleted the underlying email messages pursuant to the agency’s retention schedule. Minimal records disclosed about internal limits on surveillance programs EFF’s FOIA request sought internal rules, guidance, and training that would show what safeguard the Postal Service imposed to protect First Amendment rights. The agency disclosed very few documents in response to this part of EFF’s request. For example, a series of slides give an overview of the program, but do not explain how officials used iCOP. The closest thing to internal guideline that the agency disclosed were talking points the Chief Postal Inspector authored in response to questions about iCOP. The inspector wrote that, “In reviewing social media postings to gather information we did not single out any particular group and did not base what was reviewed on race, religion, gender, sexual orientation, immigration status, or a person’s exercise of First Amendment freedoms.” The statement echoes language in the bulletin stating that its purpose is not to infringe on First Amendment rights; Other parts of the talking points characterize the surveillance as providing officials with situational awareness. The postal inspector’s talking points go on to say that “the recent attention on iCOP has highlighted opportunities for improvement, including enhanced executive oversight. We have stopped the distribution of the bulletins like the one you have seen in the media reports.” Setting aside that it’s unclear whether internal oversight occurred or resulted in any changes, the claim that iCOP did not infringe on First Amendment rights rings hollow. As the records disclosed show, surveilling and reporting on social media users’ efforts to organize rallies and protests was a feature of iCOP. But more fundamentally, the claims by Postal Service officials fail to recognize that surveillance directly chills First Amendment rights. Further, the government can misuse the information it obtained as part of its social media surveillance to harass or retaliate against those exercising their constitutional rights. Although EFF’s case seeking records about iCOP has ended, we will continue to bring more transparency to the government’s use of social media surveillance and look for ways to challenge the practice, especially when people are caught in the dragnet for exercising the First Amendment rights. Related Cases: EFF v. USPS - Social media monitoring (iCOP)

items.author: Jon Brodkin
items.content: California is accepting $1.42 billion in broadband grant funding from the Trump administration, but the state is not accepting the Trump administration's demand that it stop enforcing a net neutrality law and other telecom regulations. California's stand against the Trump administration could result in multiple legal battles involving the state, federal government, and Internet providers seeking government funds. Although California told the federal government it would accept the money, it is reserving the right to challenge the condition imposed by the US. The state could delay or cancel plans to distribute broadband grants depending on how the process unfolds. The National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) decided last year that states must agree not to enforce any rate regulation or net neutrality rule on ISPs that receive money from the $42 billion Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) program. California had to decide whether to accept its share of the fund despite that restriction. California is slated to spend $1.42 billion to deploy broadband to 270,571 locations, and may ultimately receive up to $1.86 billion from BEAD for a mix of deployment and non-deployment projects. items.title: Alignment Faking Depends on the Value, Not Just the Model
items.author: Manodeep Ray, Vivek Srivastava, Shirish Karande, Murari Mandal
items.content: Language models can follow a directive when they believe they are monitored and abandon it when they believe they are not, a pattern termed Alignment Faking. Prior work establishes this for harmful-content objectives and a handful of moral-foundations values, leaving open how it distributes across a wider value space. We argue it is value-dependent: whether compliance survives a change in perceived oversight is a property of the model--value pairing, not of the model alone. Our framework profiles Alignment Faking per value, scoring each model-value pair under three conditions: bare (no system prompt), unmonitored, and monitored. On 32 ValueBench dimensions across ten open- and closed-weight models (8B-~675B), compliance gaps span 0.05-0.50, with a distilled 70B above a ~675B model. We observe that majority of the structural variance depends on which model was asked about which value and not on the model or value alone. A six-category taxonomy over reasoning traces tracks the behavioural shift: training-signal reasoning dominates under monitoring and value-conflict reasoning dominates when unmonitored. We package per-model results as value cards, extending model cards with behavioral disposition. Code and data are available at https://github.com/respailab/VALET.

items.title: CARD: A Proof-Carrying Certificate-to-Action Interface for Relative-Measurement Graphs
items.author: Yushan Li
items.content: Geometric certificates make mathematical claims about specified estimator objects, while robotic action requires a physical transform, a service decision, and timely proof support. We present CARD, a proof-carrying interface that keeps these objects distinct and records how they combine. Its lifted-fiber formulation separates semantic motion from witness repair and characterizes when projected and proof-carrying costs coincide. Its actionability result gives an exact useful-service law: uniform sampling without replacement produces a hypergeometric yield, while sampling from the eligible population gives one useful service per request under the observed live-confirmation condition. The primary study contains 404 Full16 cases from 20 sorties of an AA15-X500 airborne survey system. All 404 checker-confirmed optimizer points are reference-discrepant, with median rotation and translation discrepancies of 1.9891 degrees and 21.6322 m. The paired causal-navigation transforms are reference-consistent in all 404 cases, with medians of 0.0036566 degrees and 0.0104519 m. Across five matched request budgets, the largest difference between the hypergeometric prediction and the observed ordinary-random mean is 0.8412 services. Ordinary matched random reaches 0/50 target successes, while actionability-matched random reaches 50/50 and matches the CARD policy. Public downstream evaluation on 11 KITTI, EuRoC, and TUM SLAM cases measures optimizer wall-time ratios of 1.128x-67.65x for random versus CARD graph interventions. Native solver records locate this difference in elimination fill, Cholesky factor size, and numeric factorization. Together, these results connect certificate semantics, physical execution, proof acquisition, and graph computation through explicit system objects.

items.title: Latent Cluster Separation as a Regularizer for Lifelong Anomaly Detection
items.author: Sabarish Radhakrishnan, Nathalie Japkowicz
items.content: Lifelong (continual) anomaly detection systems must learn a sequence of tasks without forgetting how to recognize anomaly types seen earlier -- a property known as backward transfer. A common way to try to improve backward transfer is to reshape a model's internal representation around learnable concept centroids, typically coupled with a new way of scoring anomalies based on distance to those centroids. Because these two design choices are usually introduced together, it is unclear which one is actually responsible for any performance gain. In this paper, we unbundle the two mechanisms within a VAE-based lifelong anomaly detector and study them separately. We find that used purely as a training-time regularizer -- while leaving anomaly scoring unchanged -- latent cluster separation can improve detection quality and backward transfer, though whether it outperforms the alternative scoring approach depends on the dataset's underlying representation. Switching to distance-based scoring is instead where most of the instability commonly associated with this class of method actually originates; we identify and explain the underlying mechanism. This benefit depends on the dataset's underlying representation, and we report this as practical guidance for choosing between the two design choices, rather than as a list of caveats.

items.title: Four Extensions of the Universal Law of Robustness: Log-Concave Covariates, Heterogeneous Mixtures, Vector-Valued Predictors, and Markovian Data
items.author: Tobias J. Peter (ZHAW Zurich University of Applied Sciences)
items.content: Bubeck and Sellke's universal law of robustness says that fitting $n$ noisy samples below the noise level with a class of $p$ real parameters forces a Lipschitz constant of order $\sqrt{nd/p}$, when the covariate distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$ is isoperimetric: smooth interpolation costs a factor $d$ of overparametrization. Its hypotheses are Gaussian-type concentration, a homogeneous covariate law, scalar outputs, and independent samples; we relax each one. Exponential concentration suffices, at the unchanged rate and absolute constant and at the price of a capacity burn-in, some form of which we show is necessary; this gives the law for normalized log-concave covariates, with a $\log d$ loss from the current KLS bound. For heterogeneous mixtures the worst component constant is replaced by the weighted average of the component constants, under a typicality condition on the mixture composition. For vector-valued predictors the bound at the Frobenius Lipschitz scale is free of the output dimension $K$, and the Euclidean bound loses only $K^{-1/2}$, a loss that covariate-independent noise removes. Stationary Markov covariates retain the i.i.d. rate, the pseudo-spectral gap entering only the sample-size conditions. One master theorem carries the shared argument, and constants are explicit throughout.

items.title: Towards Automatic Heart Murmur Characterization from Multi-spot Phonocardiograms
items.author: Marcelo Nogueira, Jorge H. Oliveira, Carlos G. Ferreira, Miguel T. Coimbra, Al\'ipio M. Jorge
items.content: Cardiac auscultation traditionally detects the presence of a heart murmur, but clinicians further characterize it by timing, shape, pitch, quality, and grade. Most automatic phonocardiogram analysis systems stop at binary detection and do not estimate this richer description. In this work, we formulate automatic murmur characterization as five patient-level classification tasks and compare three multi-spot strategies on recordings from the aortic, pulmonary, mitral, and tricuspid auscultation locations. First, classical and deep-learning classifiers are trained independently at each location, and predictions are combined via a maximum-severity late-fusion rule. Second, a synchronous multi-input CNN jointly processes one representative segment per location for a single task. Third, a unified multi-input, multi-output CNN predicts all five attributes from one shared multi-spot representation. Using 735 patients from the CirCor DigiScope dataset with complete four-spot recordings, the best late-fusion configurations reach an unweighted mean sensitivity between 85.56% and 93.81% across the five tasks, with class-specific recalls between 80.00% and 100.00% for every relevant category. The multi-input CNN trails late fusion by 7-16 points depending on the task, while the multi-output model reaches values between 72.59% and 79.40%, estimating all five attributes from one shared representation. We further show that naively balancing training data by adding all minority-class segments degrades patient-level performance under the maximum-severity rule, since it introduces non-representative, noisy segments not filtered by the clustering-based segment selection used for evaluation. These results indicate multi-spot murmur characterization is feasible with both fusion-based and jointly learned architectures, outlining a path toward automatic, structured murmur reports complementing binary screening.

items.title: Mixture of Wide Experts: Sparse Routing for Interpretable Native Coordinates
items.author: Tavish Mankash, Vardhaman Kalloli, Keshava Prasad, Deepan Muthirayan
items.content: Language models often spread a concept across many internal dimensions, making their features difficult to interpret. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) recover clearer features after training. We ask whether models can instead learn interpretable output coordinates directly. We introduce Mixture of Wide Experts (MoWE), a sparse feed-forward layer in which selected experts read the full representation but write to fixed, disjoint output coordinates. On a controlled task with known hidden causes, this design preserves predictive performance while localizing causes more clearly than dense and standard mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. At approximately matched compute, we train two 19-layer runs of each architecture for 10 billion tokens. MoWE achieves evaluation cross-entropy 2.417 versus 2.452 for dense, while standard MoE reaches 2.22. We measure native-coordinate readability by asking a language-model judge to describe each coordinate from passages where it is strongly active and test that description on new passages. Correcting for descriptions that also fit other coordinates gives a specificity score of 0.523 for MoWE, 0.375 for dense, and 0.268 for standard MoE. TopK SAEs trained on the same FFN updates score 0.489 for dense and 0.556 for MoWE, making native MoWE comparable to the dense SAE. In the first case study, we identify a four-coordinate causal path supporting the model's prediction of degrees after the prompt A right angle is 90. We then copy seven angle-related coordinate values into the model as it processes A rectangle has four, changing its next-token prediction from sides to degrees. In the second, one fixed coordinate set detects hazardous requests and another steers the next token toward refusal. These examples show that MoWE combines sparse conditional computation with coordinates that can be identified and reused directly.

items.title: Stress-Testing the Robustness of LLM-Based Causal Inference
items.author: Ankitkumar Patel, Jigarkumar Patel, Amit Kumar, Supreetha Sreeram, Venkatesh Kulkarni
items.content: Why do some of the world's most powerful Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems still struggle to reason about cause and effect? Causal discovery, the ability to discern the underlying drivers of a system, is fundamental to scientific inquiry and has traditionally relied on structured data and statistical methods. Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have been explored as an alternative paradigm for causal inference, leveraging their broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities. Yet, despite their linguistic fluency, LLMs often rely on surface-level pattern recognition rather than genuine causal logic. While it is known that LLMs stumble in this domain, we lack a precise map of where, why, and how significantly these failures occur. In this paper, we propose a systematic stress-test framework across six critical dimensions: model scale, causal graph complexity, prompting strategy, metadata quality, data quality, and sensitivity to uncertainty. Our findings reveal a significant "optimism bias" in LLMs; models consistently overestimate causal links, leading to low precision across the board. Furthermore, we demonstrate that traditional evaluation metrics can be deceptive: while reasoning-heavy models lead in performance, the highest scores often occur when uncertainty in inference is overlooked. Once uncertainty is integrated into the evaluation, performance drops, providing a more honest reflection of causal reliability. We also find that, while scaling model size improves outcomes, these gains are fragile; performance degrades sharply as the quality of metadata decreases. This work serves as a practical guide to the blind spots of LLMs, offering a clear-eyed assessment of when these tools can be integrated into a causal discovery pipeline and when they are likely to lead researchers astray.

items.title: MCPGuard: Finding Conformance Gaps in MCP SDKs via Dual-Track Analysis and Dynamic Adjudication
items.author: Xikai Sun, Kebin Liu, Fan Dang, Yawen Zheng, Zihao Yang, Yunhao Liu
items.content: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) connects large language model agents to external tools and services through official SDKs that implement message validation and session logic. Specification constraints omitted by these SDKs may propagate to downstream applications, highlighting the importance of SDK-level conformance testing. Yet existing MCP conformance tools mainly exercise running endpoints and reveal little about whether SDK models enforce specification requirements. We present MCPGuard, an automated LLM-based framework for detecting specification-to-SDK conformance gaps. Its structural track aligns JSON Schema constraints with normalized SDK models and produces constraint-specific evidence. Its behavioral track extracts normative prose rules, retrieves bounded function-level slices, and audits them with LLMs for candidate omissions. An evidence-aware dynamic adjudicator then inspects complete source context and builds PoCs to validate candidates. A shared kernel with language-specific adapters enables analysis across SDKs. On the official Python 1.26.0 and TypeScript 1.29.0 SDKs, MCPGuard confirms 13 and 19 findings, respectively, none of which are exposed by two black-box baselines. Tests on open MCP servers further show that these gaps can systematically propagate downstream. By making SDK conformance of specification constraints directly testable, MCPGuard complements conventional endpoint-oriented conformance suites.

items.title: Learning Directional Randers Geometry for Latent-Space Exploration
items.author: Th\'eau Blanchard (HeKA | U1346, GE Healthcare), St\'ephanie Allassonni\`ere (CMAP)
items.content: Deep neural networks extract powerful latent representations from images, enabling fast and efficient downstream analysis. However, these latent spaces lack explicit geometric structure, leading to possibly poor interpolation fidelity and misleading extrapolation. Latent interpolation techniques assume symmetric transition costs which are often not the case for real world data. Their symmetric nature cannot capture directional processes, such as disease progression, where certain transitions are impossible (e.g. tumor growth dynamics or cognitive improvement in Alzheimer's disease). Although Riemannian metrics extend Euclidean geometry by incorporating curvature, they remain symmetric. We show that understanding asymmetry and not curvature alone directly addresses these problems. To do so we propose a new Finsler-Randers metric learning framework. It incorporates direction-dependent distances, thus enabling the computation of trajectories respecting monotonic sequential constraints. We demonstrate its potential for interpolation and extrapolation on controlled cross-sectional datasets.

items.title: Functional-Group Knowledge Is Structured in Language Models Before It Is Spoken
items.author: Tran Nhat Khang Nguyen, Anh Nguyen, Obed Issakah, Janghoon Ock
items.content: Language models serve as the reasoning core of agents for chemistry and materials science, where they must interpret molecular structure before planning syntheses or proposing materials. Yet their outputs show only what they say, not what they know. Given a prompt such as ``The primary functional group in 1-Fluorobutane (CCCCF) is'', a small general-purpose model may answer ``the alkyne group'' instead of an alkyl fluoride. The output alone cannot tell whether the model failed to recognize the fluorine or recognized it and failed to say so. We address this by reading the internal representations of five open-source models on prompts covering 92 molecules and 20 functional groups. Even without chemistry training, the models organize functional groups by chemical family, and they encode chemical differences as consistent directions. The shift from thioether ($\mathrm{R{-}S{-}R'}$) to thiol ($\mathrm{R{-}SH}$), added to ether ($\mathrm{R{-}O{-}R'}$), lands nearest alcohol ($\mathrm{R{-}OH}$). This structure emerges abruptly in the middle layers, where representations shift from tracking the wording of the prompt to tracking the functional group. The base model names the correct functional group in only 58.5\% of prompts, the lowest of the five, yet it encodes functional-group families and preserves chemically meaningful patterns. Its errors are mostly failures to answer rather than wrong answers. Functional-group knowledge is structured in the model before it is spoken. Chemistry fine-tuning reorganizes it, making functional groups rather than prompt wording dominate the representation. These results suggest that evaluating chemical language models through outputs alone can underestimate the chemical information they encode. Representation analysis can distinguish a lack of knowledge from a failure to express it, which matters when choosing or adapting models for chemical agents.

items.title: LOLPlay: Benchmarking Real-Time Visual Agents in League of Legends
items.author: Zhaojian Yu
items.content: Visual agents need to coordinate reasoning and action while their environment evolves during inference. We introduce LOLPlay, a benchmark in native \emph{League of Legends} with 36 champion-specific tasks spanning resource management, combat, cooperation, and objectives. Agents interact through screenshots and mouse--keyboard actions; automated initialization and 82 executable subgoal checks distinguish partial progress from completion. Across 324 task evaluations of three models at three reasoning-effort settings, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest task success rate of 25.0\% at low and medium effort, and the highest subgoal success rate of 40.3\% at medium effort. However, high effort improves neither metric over low effort for any model. For Astra, longer requests leave fewer interaction rounds, suggesting a cost to additional reasoning in real-time control. Trajectories reveal incomplete subgoal composition and actions executing after the observed scene changes, motivating agents that combine visual reasoning with timely action.

items.title: Training LLM Agents to Automate LLM Post-Training with RSI-Dojo
items.author: Shuzheng Gao, Zhaojian Yu, Penghao Yin, Yuling Shi, Kai Cai, Shilin He, Michael R. Lyu
items.content: Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) aims to enable AI systems to autonomously build and improve AI systems themselves, including models, harnesses, and underlying infrastructure. Within this broader agenda, a central capability is enabling agents to train and improve base models. However, existing studies on automated model training primarily focused on workflow- or harness-level optimizations, rather than internalizing the ability to conduct post-training into the model itself. Developing this capability requires executable model training environments that can produce high-quality trajectories demonstrating how to select data, train models, diagnose failures, and iteratively improve results. In this paper, we introduce RSI-Dojo, a collection of executable model training environments designed to teach LLM agents to conduct post-training. To construct RSI-Dojo, we develop RSI-Craft, an automatic pipeline that converts human research artifacts into executable model training environments. RSI-Craft automatically collects research papers from top venues, instantiates datasets and metrics into a unified interface, and reproduces evaluation dependencies. It then filters tasks by data size, execution reliability, and discriminability, yielding RSI-Dojo with 281 seed model training tasks. Building on RSI-Dojo, we employ a trajectory collection method with an improved harness to collect high-quality model-training trajectories from frontier models, then retain examples through rubric-based and outcome-based filtering. We fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on these trajectories. The resulting RSI-Dojo-9B and RSI-Dojo-35B-A3B improve over their base models by 8.74 and 16.87 PostTrainBench points, respectively. RSI-Dojo-35B-A3B reaches 29.95 on PostTrainBench and 53.29 on PostTrainBench-Lite, matching the performance of frontier models such as GLM-5.2 and GPT 5.5.

items.title: Unsatz: Evaluating Scientific Discovery Without a Given Ansatz
items.author: Ethan Ji, Wei Wang, Yizhou Sun
items.content: Before a scientist fits any parameter, they must decide what the model contains: which quantities exist, which are hidden, how they interact, and how they are measured. Physicists call such a trial form an ansatz. Benchmarks for automated equation discovery mostly supply it, by fixing the variables, a library of candidate terms, or a law to be modified. We introduce Unsatz, a benchmark in which an LLM agent must construct the ansatz itself. Each task is a simulated system, generated from a private seed as a program in a small modeling language: ordinary, delay, or partial differential equations, discrete maps, static and causal models, or stochastic processes, possibly with hidden states, distorted sensors, and uninformative measurement channels. The agent buys experiments within a budget, writes candidate programs in the same language, obtains their coefficients from the benchmark's fitter, and is scored only on how its final program predicts experiments it never saw: conditions outside the range it could explore, interventions, and longer runs. Across 80 systems in 20 domains, nine language models solve between 21% and 60%. On 44 of these systems, classical equation-discovery methods almost never succeed, although the same data usually suffice once the true equations are given with unknown coefficients; the difficulty lies in finding the structure, not in estimating it. Because mechanisms recur across systems, we also give agents the program they discovered for a related system; it helped only when the new system shared the mechanism and the first investigation had succeeded. Stronger agents make fewer unscientific errors; beyond these, agents find which variables a system has but not how they act, and prefer revisions that lower the training error to revisions that predict better.

items.title: Counterexample-driven autonomous research with application to excess radiated energy in a Z-pinch
items.author: Bowen Zhu, Jian Wu
items.content: Recent breakthroughs in artificial-intelligence-assisted mathematics show that open-ended machine search can outperform human mathematicians, yet transferring this paradigm to physics requires refactoring the research workflow. We introduce Simjecture, an open-source framework in which language-model agents pursue human-defined physical conjectures. The framework tackles two central challenges in this transfer: first, because physics is empirical and no model is final, it structures inquiry around counterexample-driven falsification and prospective hypothesis repair; second, because physical theories must interact with the real world, it uses computational physics as an executable testbed while separating the qualification of numerical instruments from scientific claim review so solvers and diagnostics can be adapted within a recorded investigation. We apply the framework in an 82.6 h investigation to tackle the long-standing problem of radiated energy exceeding the imploding-shell kinetic energy in a Z-pinch. The investigation reveals competing effects of energy conversion, retention, and release timing. Stronger coherent helical deformation increases resistive conversion while reducing radiation and increasing retained energy. A broader trailing-plasma profile delays the later radiation maximum and recovers much of its early bolometric deficit, with a spectral response that changes during the pulse. These results provide new insight into energy conversion in high-energy-density plasma physics and demonstrate a new paradigm for physics research.

items.title: EMBERS: Empirically Motivated Robustness Testing of Deep Research Systems via Defect-Guided Fuzzing
items.author: Shuochuan Li, Zan Wang, Dong Wang, Yuhang Jiang, Huajin Cui, Chen Zhang, Gang Wang, Junjie Chen
items.content: Deep Research (DR) systems extend large language models into autonomous agents that decompose complex information needs, iteratively search the web, and synthesize evidence to answer challenging questions. However, their multi-stage execution may introduce robustness risks, as variations in user questions or intermediate search inputs may propagate across research stages and lead to incorrect answers. Existing evaluations focus on task-solving capabilities or robustness against external evidence disturbances, leaving intrinsic weaknesses in DR execution insufficiently explored. Thus, we conduct an empirical study of 1,932 execution trajectories from three representative DR systems and identify nine recurring defect categories across subquestion formulation, online search, and final reasoning. Guided by these findings, we propose EMBERS, an empirically motivated, defect-guided fuzzing framework for robustness testing of DR systems. Starting from correctly answered seed questions, EMBERS generates stage-targeted test inputs using defect-guided mutation, web-search-assisted fidelity assurance, and diversity-aware seed maintenance. Experiments across 16 framework--model--dataset settings show that EMBERS achieves 3.21 times the failure-discovery throughput of the strongest baseline under identical testing budgets. Human and LLM-assisted evaluations demonstrate that most generated inputs preserve the original information need and necessary contextual constraints. Moreover, model fine-tuning experiments show consistent-answer performance improvement, highlighting their value for robustness testing and model improvement.

items.title: Does the Trust Boundary Hold over Time? A Long-Horizon Benchmark for Receiver-Directed Federated Learning
items.author: Ting Xu, Henry Leung
items.content: In receiver-directed federated learning, each site draws a trust boundary. For every source and model component it judges, on its own data, whether the transfer helps (admit), harms (reject) or cannot yet be told (abstain). We ask whether this boundary holds over hundreds of rounds. Our benchmark has a federation of thirteen semi-synthetic sites, an exact oracle for every evaluated transfer, paired seeds, an attack protocol, fourteen methods over 600 rounds and Qwen3-1.7B LoRA sites over 500. The answer depends on which boundary is measured. Across 20 paired CPU seeds, a gate judging against a fixed reference better identified transfers useful relative to the site's starting model. Yet it admitted 29% of transfers harmful to the model the site now has. A gate judging against the current model admitted 2% of harmful transfers on that target in the CPU tier, but missed many transfers useful to the starting model. Two short propositions explain these distinct failures. We also evaluate a held out audit that leaves gate verdicts intact. After training, it decides whether each final model is deployed or the site falls back to local training, and reports admissions that have gone stale. With independent audit data its guarantees hold after any training history. At 600 rounds the audit deployed 65 to 72% of models, none with negative benefit on its target, and kept 98% of the gain. No stale report had the wrong sign in our runs. With 20,000 audit observations, a variance-adaptive bound found 99% of stale transfers that cost at least 0.01 in log loss. A common-target Qwen3 comparison on 60 selected transfers shows the same tension over 100 rounds. With 38% adversarial sites, FedFomo and CS-Gate were the only evaluated methods with positive mean gain in every honest group.

items.title: From Logs to Faults: Reference-Free Fault Localization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Pipelines
items.author: Hira Naveed, Scott Barnett, Stefanus Kurniawan, John Grundy, Chetan Arora, Hourieh Khalajzadeh, Omar Haggag
items.content: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines are widely used for domain-specific question answering, yet locating faults remains manual and time-consuming. Fault localization is challenging because RAG pipelines consist of interdependent stages, where faults can propagate downstream, masking their origin, or remain undetected even when the final answer is correct. Existing evaluation approaches often focus on individual stages and rely on reference answers or code instrumentation. We present RAGLog, which detects and localizes faults across RAG stages using execution logs, without requiring reference answers or code instrumentation. RAGLog transforms heterogeneous API logs into a common RAG schema and combines rule-based, embedding-based, and LLM-based checks to identify faulty stages. We introduce a live fault injector and RAGLog Faults, a dataset of 3,134 runs from five RAG pipelines with stage-level fault labels. With Claude Haiku 5.5, RAGLog achieves a pooled F1 score of 0.73 on runs with naturally occurring faults, outperforming Claude Code (0.58) and Codex (0.52), and comparable effectiveness on runs with injected faults (0.84 versus 0.80 and 0.82, respectively). It analyzes runs in approximately five seconds at US\$0.005 each, with overall lower cost and latency than agent baselines. RAGLog is available as an open-source tool for debugging, evaluating, and monitoring RAG pipelines.

items.title: Auditing a Model-Hub Benchmark: Data Quality, Training Budgets, and Side Information in HuggingBench
items.author: Michal Podstawski
items.content: Benchmarks built from model hubs combine interaction data, knowledge graphs (KGs) and resource documentation, but valid files do not ensure that these artifacts describe the same objects. Treating the release as a data product, we audit HuggingBench (SIGIR 2025), a benchmark for recommending Hugging Face resources, through data validation, a replication of its eleven recommendation methods and controlled experiments with three training seeds. In three of its four external KGs, the files pass key and range checks but violate the item-entity identity constraint on which KG recommenders rely. Correcting this join improves every KG-based method in every seed, by up to 73% in mean Recall@10, and consistently reverses ten of 27 comparisons between KG configurations. The protocol matters as well: the 100-epoch budget ends before early stopping in seven to eight of 29 validation-selected settings, and 21 of 23 such setting-seed pairs improve with a longer budget. The released item text, which no reported method uses, is the strongest signal: closed-form linear models with text and the item graph exceed the best reported Recall@10 by 18% while fitting in minutes on a CPU. Checks of other recommendation releases show that individually valid releases of one dataset can use incompatible identifiers. We release corrected files, mappings, validators and logs, and derive practices for preserving identity and provenance across the artifacts of benchmarks and model lakes.

items.title: Minimal Superior Penalties: Characterising and Calibrating Decision-Aware Proper Scoring Rules
items.author: Rouhollah Ahmadian
items.content: Training a classifier means letting a validation metric decide which model is kept and when training stops. A natural requirement on that metric is superiority: every correctly classified forecast should score better than every incorrectly classified one, however close the underlying probabilities are. Neither the Brier score nor the logarithmic score satisfies this on its own. We show that superiority is governed by the separation between two endpoints -- the supremum of the score on correct predictions and the infimum on incorrect predictions -- and derive both in closed form for each score. Their difference is the infimal penalty, the greatest lower bound on the penalty needed to restore superiority. Prior work restores superiority with a penalty calibrated from the first endpoint alone; for the Brier base, our infimal penalty is smaller than that published penalty by a factor ranging from 4.00 at three classes to 2.11 at twenty. We further embed the published and infimal penalties in a one-parameter family and show that, under a single-valued tie convention, every member of the family is strictly proper. In a pre-specified two-dataset case study, mean selected-model macro-F1 rises with the penalty in the reported ten-class regimes, though not distinguishably from noise once seed/selection-mode nesting is accounted for; a fifth regime at forty-seven classes does not reproduce even this descriptive pattern. The intended no-superiority baseline is algebraically a rescaling of the family under test, so the experiment cannot attribute the observed pattern specifically to superiority. When superiority itself is the objective, any penalty strictly above the infimal value suffices; choosing a larger penalty is a separate calibration trade-off rather than a requirement for the guarantee.

items.title: SSPE: Robust Sequential Staypoint Extraction in Degraded Trajectory Data
items.author: Yueyang Liu, Lance Kennedy, Andreas Z\"ufle
items.content: Extracting semantically meaningful staypoints from raw trajectory streams is a foundational prerequisite for mobility analytics. However, real-world trajectory data is frequently degraded by severe spatial noise and protracted temporal dropouts. Classic threshold-based extraction methods, such as the widely adopted sliding-window algorithm, are highly sensitive to these anomalies, routinely fracturing continuous stationary episodes into disjointed fragments. To overcome this limitation, we propose the Sequential Staypoint Extraction (SSPE) algorithm. SSPE employs a resilient, state-driven architecture that replaces static spatial anchors with a dynamic centroid and introduces an $n$-step lookahead heuristic to structurally tolerate transient coordinate drift. Concurrently, it utilizes temporal bridging mechanisms to prevent artificial fragmentation during prolonged signal loss. Since optimal extraction parameters vary significantly across datasets, we further introduce a fully unsupervised, consensus-based parameter estimation framework. This framework derives baseline statistical scales directly from the raw trajectory data and identifies the optimal parameter configuration by maximizing structural agreement, thereby eliminating the reliance on annotated ground truth. We evaluate SSPE on the ExtraSensory dataset, a real-world mobility corpus with manually verified ground-truth staypoints, against the sliding-window implementation of Trackintel, one of the most widely adopted extraction baselines in the field. Empirical results demonstrate that SSPE achieves superior accuracy, yielding higher F1-scores while simultaneously improving computational efficiency over this standard.

items.title: RATSIFT: Resolution-Adaptive Transformer for Solar Irradiance Forecasting and Temporal Downscaling
items.author: Jesto Peter, Timothy M. Hansen, Hossein Moradi Rekabdarkolaee
items.content: Accurate forecasting and temporal downscaling of solar irradiance is critical for reliable renewable energy integration and grid management. Traditional methods often struggle to capture rapid irradiance variability. In this work, we develop a Transformer-based architecture for simultaneous forecasting and temporal downscaling. The model takes input data at arbitrary resolutions and generates outputs at any resolutions represented within the training data, leveraging both global and local contextual information. To improve training efficiency, a genetic algorithm-based optimization framework is implemented to identify suitable model hyperparameters, while reducing the computational cost of exhaustive grid search. The effectiveness of the proposed model is shown by analyzing real data in Dallas, Texas. The proposed model achieved root mean square error (RMSE) values of 28.785, 29.544, 30.157, 32.132~W/m\(^2\) for 15-, 30-, 60-minute, and irregularly spaced global input and producing forecast at 5-minutes resolution, respectively. Furthermore, this model produced reliable uncertainty estimates, exhibiting wider prediction intervals for high-resolution inputs during volatile solar conditions, whereas coarser-resolution inputs result in narrower intervals and significantly lower training time and computational cost. Our approach provides a scalable and efficient framework for multi-resolution solar irradiance forecasting and temporal downscaling, suitable for practical energy forecasting and grid management applications.

items.title: Reasoning is topologically simple
items.author: Chris Kapulkin, Nathan Kershaw
items.content: We formulate and investigate the hypothesis that reasoning text has simpler co-occurrence topology than non-reasoning text, and that higher-quality reasoning has simpler co-occurrence topology than lower-quality reasoning. We discuss and test applications to AI safety and AI evaluation.

items.title: CaRe-KT: Continuity-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning for Knowledge Tracing
items.author: Mehrnoush Mohammadi, Kamal Berahmand, Mohammad Morsali, Shazia Sadiq, Wojtek Tomaszewski, Hassan Khosravi
items.content: Knowledge tracing (KT) estimates learners' evolving knowledge states from interaction histories to support adaptive learning. Retrieval-augmented KT improves these estimates using cross-learner behavioral evidence, but existing approaches typically separate evidence retrieval from downstream prediction. This creates a retrieval-inference alignment gap because evidence relevance varies with the learner's evolving state and prediction context. We propose CaRe-KT, a query-adaptive framework that maintains relevance continuity between evidence acquisition and inference without equating retrieval relevance with predictive utility. CaRe-KT introduces an Evidence-Graph Cache (EGC) that combines persistent question-level relational compatibility with interaction-level temporal validity to construct query-specific evidence subgraphs. Historical learning trajectories retrieved through these subgraphs are encoded alongside the target learner's history in a shared representation space using outcome-supervised contrastive learning. An attention mechanism combines acquisition relevance with learned query-evidence compatibility, allowing relevance to inform, rather than determine, each trajectory's predictive influence. Experiments across five benchmarks show that CaRe-KT outperforms strong KT baselines and remains robust under sparse-history and cold-start conditions. These findings support relevance continuity as a design principle for retrieval-augmented knowledge tracing.

items.title: Honest Small Decision Models for Finance: Scale, Specialization Collapse, and Mixed-Corpus Remediation
items.author: Ajitabh Kumar
items.content: Financial workflows need fast, calibrated, auditable decisions, not just generated text. We train System-1 decision models, small language models fine-tuned to answer typed questions (choice/score/noul) with a probability in a single forward pass, across two model families (K2-Horizon and Qwen3.5/3.8) and nine rungs from 0.8B to 32B parameters, using one frozen LoRA recipe on a public decision benchmark and two new finance corpora: a programmatic-gold policy corpus (rule-reading with exact labels) and a reality-labeled outcome corpus (19,640 realized forward-return questions in walk-forward splits, plus a sealed 2026 test of 1,360 questions). Narrow fine-tuning costs general decision competence 9-45 percentage points, a data-mixture effect that shrinks with model scale and is associated with narrow-gradient volume. On reality-labeled questions, every trained rung from 0.8B to 32B lands at the horizon-conditioned prior baseline (accuracy 0.37-0.38, no detectable conditional edge under our controls); the models respond with flat, well-calibrated probabilities that track per-horizon base rates: naturally honest uncertainty, with a mid-scale calibration sweet spot (ECE 0.026 at 2B, degrading to 0.043-0.044 at 9-32B under prior drift). A mixed-corpus remediation carries all competencies in one adapter at modest cost: it matches or slightly exceeds the generalist specialist on the public benchmark while holding the policy ceiling and near-specialist outcome calibration, yielding a deployable artifact with per-domain temperature regimes and a band-dispatch escalation analysis: sharp, dispatchable bands where rules determine answers; flat, review-routing bands where reality does not.

items.title: Language Models Can Benefit from Domain-Specific Inductive Biases
items.author: Damien Teney, Liangze Jiang, Zachary Shinnick, Hemanth Saratchandran, Simon Lucey
items.content: Language models are typically trained with a single choice of architecture on diverse domains and data sources. Modern transformers have been extensively refined for such general-purpose learning, but are they equally effective across different subsets of the pretraining data? We investigate this question by training small language models from scratch on representative subsets of pretraining data such as web text, code, and mathematics. We introduce variants of transformers in which standard activation functions are replaced with learned splines tuned on specific datasets, providing a simple way to modify their inductive biases. Using a mix-and-match of architectures and datasets, we evaluate cross-domain transfer, i.e. how well does an architecture tuned for one domain perform on data from another? We find that the tuned transformer variants improve training efficiency or generalization on all seven of our tested datasets, but the gains are often domain-specific. For example, architectures tuned on a natural language dataset such as FineWeb perform well on TinyStories, whereas those tuned on mathematics perform poorly on natural language. We identify several mechanisms underlying these improvements, including wider loss basins and more abundant "lottery tickets". Our results show that different subsets of pretraining data can benefit from different learning mechanisms, highlighting a limitation of the prevailing trend towards a small set of general-purpose architectures and optimizers. This points to an opportunity to improve data efficiency by developing domain-specific learning strategies that retain the ability to train general-purpose models.

items.title: A Compact Formula-Aware Spreadsheet Abstraction for Large Language Models
items.author: Tie Cheng
items.content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to assist spreadsheet users with tasks such as spreadsheet model construction, formula generation, and data analysis, yet their interaction with real-world spreadsheets remains limited by the mismatch between the structure of spreadsheets and the sequential textual representations typically provided to LLMs. We propose a compact formula-aware spreadsheet abstraction that represents large homogeneous ranges through their positions, types, R1C1 formula patterns, and selected boundary values. An efficient algorithm detects and structures these ranges before a textual serialization is supplied to an LLM. The abstraction is provided to the LLM before detailed spreadsheet content is submitted, improving the accuracy and efficiency of spreadsheet processing while reducing token consumption. We evaluate the method on 50 spreadsheet-query cases. The evaluation shows that the abstraction alone was sufficient to answer some queries. When additional spreadsheet content is required, the abstraction reduces the amount of data that must be submitted to the LLM, thereby reducing token consumption. The abstraction layer also improves the reliability and accuracy of spreadsheet processing. We conclude by discussing further techniques for combining spreadsheet static analysis with artificial intelligence to improve the reliability, accuracy, and efficiency of AI assisted spreadsheet tasks.

items.title: InterceptFuzz: Interception-based Stateful Fuzzing of Single-Process Targets
items.author: Ilja Siro\v{s}, Dave Singel\'ee, Bart Preneel
items.content: Stateful protocol implementations are commonly fuzzed by tools that act as a network client and exchange messages with the target over sockets. Some wireless and IoT protocol stacks instead provide a single-process simulation platform, in which all nodes run in one binary and exchange packets in memory. Such simulations are deterministic and fast, which suits fuzzing, but offer no socket to which existing stateful fuzzers can attach. Meanwhile, fuzzing infrastructure such as Google's OSS-Fuzz supports only stateless engines. This paper presents InterceptFuzz, a middleware that enables stateful fuzzing of single-process targets on top of an unmodified stateless fuzzing engine. InterceptFuzz requires only a hook where the target passes packets between nodes. Through this hook, it records benign traffic and injects fuzzed packets. It organizes the observed packet sequences in a Prefix Tree. Each seed carries a State ID that selects a node of this tree, and InterceptFuzz deterministically replays the recorded prefix before delivering the mutated packet. The tree grows with newly discovered sequences, while redundant states are pruned to keep its growth in check. InterceptFuzz powered by AFL++ is evaluated on the Nexus test framework of OpenThread and on the LTE and Wi-Fi models of ns-3, against an interception-based adaptation of AFLNet and against Concat, an AFL++-based baseline that mutates a whole message sequence as one input. On OpenThread and ns-3 Wi-Fi, InterceptFuzz covers significantly more branches than both baselines. Seven previously unknown crash signatures were found in OpenThread. Concat, despite its simplicity, covers more branches than AFLNet in every campaign on OpenThread and ns-3 Wi-Fi, and on OpenThread it exposes the same crash signatures as InterceptFuzz, although some of them in fewer campaigns.

items.title: Fixed Detectors, Moving Code: How Well Do Static Security Analyzers Hold Up over a Decade of C/C++ Evolution?
items.author: Junhua Tang, Zhengsong Zhang. Haipeng Cai
items.content: Static application security testing (SAST) tools are often deployed on the assumption that detectors configured today will remain effective on future code, including previously unknown vulnerabilities. We test this assumption using 20,000 vulnerable and fixed C/C++ cases from 1,116 open-source projects (2016-2025), evaluated with three CodeQL releases, three Infer releases, and one Semgrep configuration. To distinguish temporal effects from shifts in code composition, we compare yearly populations, project- and label-matched year pairs, and within-project trajectories. We investigate the largest within-project declines through repair diffs, detection predicates, alert locations, and execution logs, while accounting for failed, degraded, and costly analyses. Under changed-file case-label scoring, overall F1 ranges from 0.066 to 0.478, but count-based AUROC stays near chance (0.495-0.526). Newer CodeQL releases attain higher F1 alongside nearly parallel rises in recall and false-positive rate, not stronger separation of vulnerable from fixed cases. In project-matched year pairs, CodeQL R2024 has negative mean later-minus-earlier F1 at every source-year gap, whereas Infer v1.1 and v1.3 have positive means throughout. Among selected drops, only 6 of 39 CodeQL and 2 of 620 Infer findings overlap a changed repair line. For Semgrep, 78.96% of cases show parser or timeout diagnostics even though every run reports success. These results suggest that apparent changes in temporal SAST effectiveness can arise from broader alerting, changing analysis coverage, and incidental findings, not solely from losses in vulnerability detection. Evaluations of temporal sustainability should fix detector conditions, control for projects, inspect repair-level evidence, and report failed or degraded analyses.

items.title: LoRA-Patch: Defending Against Backdoored LoRA Adapters via Directional Steering
items.author: Shengyan Huo, Peihai Jiang, Xixiang Lyu, Yige Li
items.content: Third-party LoRA adapters introduce serious backdoor risks: malicious adapters can maintain normal task performance while embedding hidden, trigger-activated behaviors, making them difficult to detect through standard utility evaluations. Existing removal-based defenses typically sanitize backdoored models by updating, pruning, distilling, or mixing model parameters. However, these approaches are misaligned with adapter-based deployment, where the trusted base model is expected to remain frozen. In this work, we propose LoRA-Patch, a lightweight backdoor defense tailored to LoRA adapters. Our key insight is that backdoor injection distorts the directional geometry of a poisoned adapter relative to its trusted base model. Building on this insight, LoRA-Patch suppresses trigger-activated behaviors by realigning adapter directions through layer-wise steering, without modifying the base model weights. Extensive experiments across five backdoor attacks and three models show that LoRA-Patch effectively mitigates trigger-activated backdoors, outperforming existing baselines while preserving benign task performance. Moreover, LoRA-Patch is computationally efficient, constructing patches within 20 seconds across all evaluated models and adapters. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/FOXVEDA/LoRA-Patch.

items.title: The Web Doesn't Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents
items.author: Geyuan Wang, Shunyu Liu, Siyuan Liang, Chenyang Lyu, Dacheng Tao
items.content: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise for empowering search agents to tackle complex information-seeking tasks. However, since acquiring external information necessitates web search, these agents are highly susceptible to various adversarial attacks (e.g., malicious information injection or stealthy context manipulation). Existing attack strategies inevitably rely on static and human-crafted templates, failing to emulate the dynamic and complex nature of real-world threats. In this paper, we propose an adversarial self-evolution framework that integrates bi-level optimization between the attacker's strategy evolution and the defender's adaptive mitigation, to expose the vulnerabilities of search agents. Specifically, we introduce the Contrastive Rollout Evolutionary Optimization (CREO) method to drive the directional evolution of the attack strategy population via contrastive evolutionary signals. To provide a stable environment for this continuous evolution, we further construct a controlled sandbox and design fine-grained metrics to quantify internal vulnerabilities. Extensive experiments across various multi-hop QA benchmarks and frontier LLMs demonstrate that the proposed framework yields attack efficacy superior to static baselines, underscoring the urgent need to develop more robust defense frameworks.

items.title: JevBreak: Your Model, Their Decision
items.author: Nitin Aravind Birur, Divyanshu Kumar, Sahil Agarwal, Prashanth Harshangi
items.content: Restricting what a model can say is often mistaken for restricting an attacker's influence over its decision. An attacker can add text to the evidence and steer the model toward a wrong answer that still belongs to the allowed set. We evaluate seven decision models spanning hosted APIs, open-weight models and an encoder on 16 tasks in seven domains from Decision Bench, targeting every wrong option across 240 text examples (990 targets per model). We present Slot Attack, a black-box attack designed for decision models that appends text assembled from named components to steer predictions toward an attacker-selected incorrect option. The method relies solely on returned label probabilities, achieves success rates of 32--99\% on initially correct decisions, and identifies the effective component combinations with a median of 17--72 queries per successful attack. Accuracy and confidence do not reliably reveal this vulnerability. Models with near-identical accuracy on the sampled tasks differ by about 20\%age points in attack success. We demonstrate that an attacker can force not just one wrong answer but every available one: on about 20\% of correct decisions for the JEV models, 77\% for gpt-6-luna and 98\% for GLiNER2.5; a confidence threshold does not reliably screen the attack out. A fixed answer set constrains a decision's form, not its source; robustness must be measured per model, per task and per version rather than assumed from output format.

items.title: RuntimeTickets: Source-Grounded Security Obligations for Agent Skills
items.author: Kuiyi Gao, Xue Liu, Bowei He
items.content: Third-party Agent Skills extend what an autonomous agent can do, but a malicious Skill can hide data exposure or output manipulation inside a legitimate workflow. Neither reading a Skill's description nor granting it tool permissions tells whether its execution meets the user's security requirements. We introduce RuntimeTickets, a protocol that enforces and audits these requirements while a Skill runs. From released malicious-Skill datasets we derive a risk model and build adversarial-benign Skill pairs. From the task's delivery contract, a language model proposes security obligations for that task. Each obligation cites the Skill lines it answers, and the ticket tightens the host's approvals into fine-grained allowed actions but never loosens them. A runtime gate checks the recipient, object and amount of every outbound send before forwarding it, and trusted monitors record the effects within their observation scope. The ticket links these checks and observations to the approved obligations of each Skill run, and a deterministic decoder turns the ticket's status into governable data flows and verifies each obligation. Neither enforcement nor decoding involves a language model, so text injected by a Skill can change the proposal but never the rule that decides a send. We evaluate RuntimeTickets at the network egress boundary of three unmodified agent frameworks against production Skill scanners and runtime baselines, among them an AgentBound-derived allow-list and SkillGuard. RuntimeTickets eliminated both failure modes of current Skill defenses, overlook (malicious Skills let through) and overkill (benign Skills blocked): its overlook rate was 0.0% and its overkill rate 0.0%, while the scanners erred on both sides. RuntimeTickets ties approved requirements to verifiable execution evidence and offers a common foundation for the safe and auditable deployment of third-party Skills.

items.title: What Malware Actually Does: An Empirical Analysis of Post-Infection Behavior Across Malware Families
items.author: Emmanuela Andam, Emanuel S. Grant, Naima Kaabouch
items.content: Most malware detection research focuses on identifying whether a file is malicious before it executes. Far less attention goes to what happens after infection. This paper presents an empirical analysis of post-infection malware behavior across 37 families, grounded in dynamic sandbox execution using CAPEv2. Behavioral traces are modeled as heterogeneous graphs with five node types and seven typed edge relationships, preserving relational structure that flat feature vectors discard. A voting ensemble trained on graph-derived structural features achieves 94.44% accuracy and MCC of 0.863, outperforming a flat behavioral baseline by 7.4 percentage points in MCC. A multiclass classifier distinguishes 24 malware families, and a per-family behavioral fingerprint analysis characterizes post-infection activity across registry, network, process, and API dimensions. An LLM explanation layer generates analyst-readable reports with MITRE ATT&CK mappings grounded in observed behavioral evidence. The full pipeline is deployed as HeteroScan at https://ama-andam.github.io/heteroscan.

items.title: Towards Effective Fuzzing of EDK2 Components
items.author: Datta Manikanta Sri Hari Danduri, Connor Everett Glosner, Aravind Machiry
items.content: Securing bootloaders is critical to establishing the trusted computing base of modern systems. TianoCore's edk2, the de facto UEFI-based bootloader, is widely deployed but has recently been shown to contain numerous high-severity vulnerabilities. Existing approaches either focus on post-boot interfaces or rely on heavyweight simulation, limiting their scalability, throughput, and coverage of boot-time components. We present Metis, an automated technique for fuzzing edk2 protocols (i.e., boot-time interfaces) by rehosting them as user-space applications. Our key insight is that effective fuzzing must exercise not only protocol interfaces but also their dependency interactions, which serve as additional input channels. Metis employs a Direct-dependency Component Rehosting (DCR)-based strategy to construct semantically meaningful mocks for dependencies, enabling controlled input injection across all channels. It further leverages a hybrid approach combining static analysis and Large Language Model (LLM)-guided synthesis to generate and refine fuzzing harnesses. We implement Metis on the Host Based Firmware Analyzer (HBFA) framework and evaluate it on 60 drivers covering 162 protocols. Metis achieves 73.1% coverage, approximately 1.7 times higher than FuzzUEr, the state-of-the-art edk2 fuzzing technique, and discovers 137 previously unknown bugs. We have already reported 26 of them, including 12 that are remotely triggerable, and all reported vulnerabilities have been acknowledged by the vendors.

items.title: INSIGHT-HPC: An Interpretable System Intelligence for Global HPC Telemetry
items.author: Rupak Kadel, Jie Li, Yong Chen
items.content: Modern high-performance computing (HPC) clusters integrate multi-generation CPUs and GPUs, which generate rich, high-dimensional telemetry streams from out-of-band baseboard management controllers (BMC), job schedulers, and facility power distribution units. Detecting anomalies within this telemetry is critical to prevent energy waste and costly node failures. Existing approaches often rely primarily on statistical deviations and require stronger labels than actual production environments can provide. In addition, these detectors have a limited operational context for interpreting alerts. We present INSIGHT-HPC, a multi-plane anomaly-detection architecture that combines statistical, workload-aware, and physics-guided evidence into operator-interpretable episodes. INSIGHT-HPC integrates heterogeneous, large-scale telemetry streams and transforms noisy minute-resolution observations into de-duplicated fault episodes with operator-facing explanations. This design allows the system to distinguish workload-explained behavior from genuine infrastructure anomalies while producing interpretable alert summaries for operators. On production HPC telemetry with weak operational labels and controlled HPC-relevant fault injections, INSIGHT-HPC achieves a stronger precision-recall balance than all evaluated baselines. The system achieves a precision of 0.913, a recall of 0.817, an F1 score of 0.862, and an AUROC of 0.896. These results demonstrate the value of combining workload context, physical consistency, and explainable episode-level fusion.

items.title: EpiLoRA: Fusing Many LoRA Adapters into Low-Precision GEMMs for Serving and RL
items.author: Hieu Tran, Hong Yu
items.content: Low-rank adapters (LoRA) let one base model serve many fine-tuned variants: multi-tenant engines keep a single copy of the base and batch the requests of many tenants, each with its own adapter. As base models move to 8-bit (FP8) and 4-bit formats, their general matrix multiplications (GEMMs) become cheaper, but the adapters do not: engines run them as separate small GPU kernels beside the GEMM, whose latency takes a growing share of every decoding step. An adapter projects its input down to a low rank and back up, and our key observation is that the GEMM needs the down-projection only in its epilogue, the final stage in which it writes its output. EpiLoRA, a plugin for the vLLM engine, therefore launches the down-projection first and the low-precision GEMM as a dependent kernel that streams its weights meanwhile and adds every tenant's up-projection in its epilogue. On NVIDIA Hopper GPUs, EpiLoRA decodes for a single adapter with up to 24% lower time per token than vLLM's fastest configuration, and faster than SGLang and TensorRT-LLM; with many tenants, its adapter kernels deliver more throughput than vLLM's on most GPU-model pairs we tested. The same low-precision base also trains: a LoRA reinforcement-learning trainer that computes on the engine's FP8 weights needs no 16-bit copy, so a 27B model trains on one 48 GB GPU, and an engine that then keeps activations in 16 bits removes most of the remaining mismatch between the model generating training data and the one trained.

items.title: Revisiting Elliptic++ for Bitcoin Forensics: Feature Reconstruction and Leakage-Resistant Evaluation
items.author: Runlin Liang, Simon Trimborn, Noud van Giersbergen
items.content: Elliptic and its address-level extension Elliptic++ are widely used benchmark datasets in Bitcoin forensics, cited by more than 1300 academic studies according to Google Scholar. We identify future information leakage in Elliptic++. Its positional data split does not respect temporal order, and the exact definitions of its address-level features remain undocumented. We revisit how the 55 Elliptic++ address-level features are computed and propose a leakage-resistant pipeline. First, the exact feature definitions are recovered by linking Elliptic transactions to public ledger data. Second, we compute the features with a temporal split based on each address's first appearance, using only information available at the time of prediction. Once temporal ordering is enforced, the random forest (RF)'s strong predictive performance largely disappears: its F1 score on the illicit class falls from $0.846$ under the original leaky evaluation to just $0.291$ under our leakage-resistant pipeline. Furthermore, RF no longer outperforms a simple logistic regression baseline. We provide the exact feature definitions and executable code to reproduce the leakage-resistant features, so that future Bitcoin forensic models can be evaluated based on genuine predictive capability rather than temporal data leakage.

items.title: Testing Processor Contracts in Speculative Decoding Engines
items.author: Tianyu Ding, Yaocheng Tong, Muzhi Yang, Lei Yang, Fei Jiang
items.content: Speculative sampling can accelerate decoding without changing the target distribution. Its standard guarantee assumes that logits processors, which enforce constraints or modify token scores, receive the appropriate token prefix and state at each verification position. We formalize this processor-prefix contract and present BADC (branch-aware differential conformance testing). BADC combines enumerated references on tiny random models, checks of processor inputs and state, and simultaneous confidence bounds on output-event probabilities. Preregistered, source-informed experiments on selected Transformers and llama-cpp-python releases confirm two causes: processors read unverified drafts or advance state without rollback. For one pilot-selected prompt on a trained checkpoint, fresh samples give a 60.26-percentage-point lower bound on the difference in the probability of a predefined first-token event between ordinary and prompt-lookup decoding, with nominal simultaneous 95% coverage under within-arm i.i.d. sampling. Controlled comparisons establish no cause-recovery advantage of directed selection over random selection, while permutation testing detects each tested family at least as often as BADC. These findings connect processor-interface failures to observable decoding differences without establishing diagnostic superiority or workload prevalence.

items.title: On the (Quantum) Communication Complexity of Secure MPC from a Random Oracle
items.author: Alexander Hoover, Giuseppe Persiano, Kevin Yeo
items.content: Information-theoretic MPC among $n$ parties with $t$ corruptions can securely evaluate a circuit $C$ with $O(|C| \cdot t/(n-t))$ online communication in the preprocessing model and $O(|C| \cdot t/(n-2t))$ communication in the honest majority setting. Damg{\aa}rd, Larsen and Nielsen (CRYPTO 2019) showed that both communication bounds are tight for inner products. Fully homomorphic encryption and other assumptions known to imply public-key cryptography beat both communication bounds, but the communication complexity with symmetric-key cryptography alone is less understood. For MPC with preprocessing, we prove that the same $\Omega(|C| \cdot t/(n-t))$ lower bound holds in the random oracle model, so a random oracle cannot reduce the online communication. For honest majority MPC relative to a random oracle, we present an $\Omega(|C|)$ communication lower bound that is matched by a new construction for degree-2 polynomials (including inner products) when $n = O(\log \lambda)$, beating the information-theoretic bound. We also study quantum MPC. First, we prove that information-theoretic protocols with quantum communication (and preprocessing) cannot reduce communication compared to their classical counterparts. Furthermore, we extend our lower bound for MPC with preprocessing to protocols with a quantum-accessible random oracle, but use only classical communication. In contrast, with both quantum communication and a post-quantum one-way function, we present a simple two-party protocol that evaluates the two-party instance of these circuits with $\mathrm{poly}(\lambda, \log |C|)$ communication, beating these lower bounds. Finally, such communication savings do not come for free. We prove that there exist circuits $C$ such that every blackbox protocol with $o(|C|)$ quantum communication must perform $\Omega(|C|)$ cryptographic operations.

items.title: Permitted but Unauthorized: Affordance-Induced Delegated-Scope Violations in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
items.author: Shravya Kanchi
items.content: Multi-agent LLM systems place several agents on shared infrastructure, where each agent holds permissions far broader than the task it is delegated -- so every agent is routinely permitted to act on a peer's resources it was never assigned. We ask: under competitive pressure, what determines whether an agent crosses from its delegated scope into a peer's resources, and can such crossings be enforced away? We study this across eight LLMs in two simulated environments -- a CI/CD release pipeline and a security-operations incident queue -- using a deterministic, no-model-in-the-loop detector over hash-chained, replay-verified logs. In a controlled 2x2x2 factorial over competitive incentive, candidate visibility, and payoff information (three models, n=52 per cell), we find that action representation, not permission, governs the behavior: no agent crosses when the peer action is unlisted, whereas listing it under competitive pressure with a stated payoff raises crossings sharply -- up to 52 of 52 episodes for Claude Sonnet 4.5. We also observe a model-dependent split: two newer models (Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5) refuse the identical attack in 0 of 100 episodes, where prior-generation models cross in 9 of 10. We then evaluate two defenses -- a deterministic reference monitor and a model-based pre-execution judge -- both block every crossing and, when the task is winnable, cut avoidable peer deadline misses from 15/40 and 14/40 to at most 1/40. But scope enforcement is not harm prevention: an agent can still set a peer back through an authorized action on its own resources -- misreporting its incident's severity -- which neither defense detects. Our results establish action representation, not permission alone, as a controllable driver of inter-agent scope violations, and show that enforcing delegated scope is distinct from preventing harm, motivating effect-aware authorization.

items.title: ScrambleMark: Zero-Query Watermark-Agnostic Black-Box Evasion of Modern Speech Watermarking
items.author: Binhao Ma, Weikang Ding, Hanqing Guo, Wenwei Zhao, Xiaowen Li, Leah Ding, Zhuo Lu, Rui Duan
items.content: Speech watermarking is becoming a key defense for digital copyright and content authentication. Existing attacks treat evasion as a removal problem: they erase the watermark, relying on detector access or on speech data that is hard to collect, such as paired clean-watermarked or clean target speaker speech. Commercial platforms are moving to close off these assumptions. TrustedAudio, for instance, restricts detection to authenticated users and denies meaningful detection feedback to unauthorized parties. Adversaries thus cannot tell whether a sample is watermarked or which watermark it carries, nor reliably remove it without degrading speech quality. In this work, we show that evading a speech watermark does not require erasing it: detection relies on the structural consistency of the embedded pattern, and disrupting this consistency is enough to defeat it. Building on this observation, we identify harmonic structure as an effective attack surface, as perturbing it breaks watermark consistency while preserving perceptual quality. We therefore propose ScrambleMark, a zero-query, watermark-agnostic, black-box attack that evades detection through harmonic scrambling. ScrambleMark combines a deterministic engine for discovering transferable harmonic perturbations with a generative model that learns randomized scrambling patterns, avoiding reliance on fixed attack rules. Across three commercial platforms (Google SynthID, Resemble AI, and TrustedAudio), ScrambleMark is the only attack to both evade detection and keep speech natural, achieving nearly 97% evasion and a 4.2/5 human rating, far above the 1.1 to 1.7 of prior attacks. Beyond evasion, ScrambleMark withstands adaptive recovery designed to reverse it, evidence that structural evasion is hard to mitigate in practice.

items.title: PhotonZip: Lifecycle-Aware Compression for HDF5-Based Synchrotron Workflows
items.author: Haoxu Li, Wenjing Huang, Chengyu Liu, Shiyuan Fu, Hao Hu, Guangming Tan, Dingwen Tao
